newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Nigerian election time change amplifies doubts.
newsitem.headline: Nigerian election time change amplifies doubts.

text.p: Changes to the timetable for elections in Nigeria have added to doubts about the commitment of its military rulers to restoring democracy, opponents and analysts said on Thursday.

"The administration has not kept faith with the timely implementation of some its key components, a situation which has continually raised suspicion over the genuine intention of the administration," wrote Yusuph Olaniyonu in the independent Thisday newspaper.

Since military leader General Sani Abacha in 1995 set out his timetable for a return to civilian rule in Africa's most populous nation, his plan has been attacked as insincere at every stage, by critics both at home and abroad.
The committee handling the transition plan said on Wednesday elections scheduled for this year had been put off until next year at the request of the five legal political parties.
Presidential elections are set for August 1, before a promised handover to civilian rule on October 1, 1998.
"We are being vindicated. How many times have they shifted? I don't even know," said Ganiyu Dawodu, a senior figure in the umbrella National Democratic Coalition (NADECO), opposed to Abacha's rule.

Opponents say the democracy plan, adopted when Nigeria was under severe national and international pressure to reform, is no more than a ruse to ensure the military retains power in the West African oil giant.
Abacha's supporters are urging him to stand in the presidential poll and become an elected civilian ruler, following in the path of many of his regional colleagues.

So far the infantry general has not said he would take part, but opponents believe he will, and political analysts say the reason other possible contenders have not thrown their hats into the ring is because they are waiting to see what Abacha does.

The army, which has ruled Africa's most populous nation for 27 out of its 37 years of independence from Britain, annulled a presidential vote in 1993 which would have restored democracy, plunging Nigeria into political and economic crisis.
Wealthy businessman Moshood Abiola, the presumed winner of the annulled poll, has been detained since 1994 when he declared himself president and his treason trial is yet to begin.

Former Western allies have isolated Nigeria for human rights abuses and the slow pace of its democratic reform, and the new timetable change has done nothing to convince them they may have been too harsh.
"In itself the change is not necessarily important, but if you don't respect a timetable then why respect other promises?" said one senior Western diplomat in Lagos.
Nigeria was suspended from the Commonwealth in 1995 after it defied international opinion and hanged nine minority rights activists, including author Ken Saro-Wiwa.
British Foreign Secretary Robin Cook last month made a stinging attack on Abacha's governmnent, saying nothing had happened in the country to warrant lifting the suspension.
